questions.q: What is the protagonist's name in "Ajamil and the Tigers," and what is his primary occupation as stated in the poem?
questions.a: The protagonist is Ajamil, a shepherd. A wrong answer (e.g., naming the tiger king or sheepdog) reveals the student cannot identify the central human figure around whom the allegory revolves, indicating they haven't grasped the poem's narrative perspective.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Ajamil refuses to meet the sheepdog's eyes after the tigers are captured.
questions.a: Ajamil avoids the sheepdog's eyes because the dog's honest outrage exposes Ajamil's deliberate choice to betray his loyal protector for a convenient pact with the tigers. A wrong answer suggesting "fear" or "shame" misses the calculated nature of Ajamil's complicity — he isn't embarrassed; he's strategically ignoring truth to maintain his narrative.

questions.q: Apply the allegorical framework (sheep = citizens, tigers = corrupt politicians, sheepdog = judiciary/law enforcement) to explain what Ajamil's signing of the "friendship treaty" represents in real-world politics.
questions.a: The treaty represents a politician legitimizing criminal elements through formal agreements (like coalitions with tainted parties) to secure short-term stability, sacrificing institutional integrity (sheepdog) and public welfare (sheep). An incomplete answer would only describe the plot event without mapping it to the political reality the allegory critiques.

questions.q: Analyze the significance of the line "Ajamil wasn't a fool. Like all good shepherds he knew that even tigers have got to eat some time." How does this redefine "good shepherd" in the poem's logic?
questions.a: The line redefines "good shepherd" not as protector of the flock but as manager of predators — a leader who sustains power by feeding corrupt forces (tigers) portions of public resources (sheep) to prevent total destruction. A surface reading misses the irony: the poem calls this "good shepherding" to expose how political vocabulary corrupts moral language.

questions.q: Evaluate whether Ajamil is a tragic figure forced by circumstances or a morally culpable enabler. Support your judgment with two specific textual evidences.
questions.a: Ajamil is morally culpable: (1) He "pretended to believe every single word" of the tiger king's lies, showing conscious deception, not coercion. (2) He actively "cut them loose" and hosted dinner, initiating the treaty. A student calling him "helpless" ignores his agency in choosing compromise over resistance when the sheepdog had already won.

questions.q: Create a 4-line dialogue between Ajamil and the sheepdog that reveals their conflicting worldviews, using the poem's tone of ironic understatement.
questions.a:
Sheepdog: "They had you at their mercy, master. I held them."
Ajamil: "And now they're friends. The flock loses less this way."
Sheepdog: "You fed them lamb chops from my flock."
Ajamil: "A shepherd feeds wolves to keep the peace, dog. Count the sheep tomorrow."
A weak answer makes the conflict explicit and emotional; the poem's power lies in Ajamil's cold, bureaucratic tone.
